Entries that list layers no longer open (left under a route an action pushed before its layer closed, or from before a reload) are stepped over in the direction the user went, so neither Back nor Forward lands on a dead entry. On the web it is on for a touch pointer only, never in Electron: with a mouse, the browser's Back keeps its plain meaning. The open thread is not a layer: it has its own route entry (?thread=), so Back already closes it.
  • The opener when nothing had focus. Some platforms do not focus a button when it is clicked (Safari). When focus is on the page body as a layer opens, the opener is the layer's own fallback (a Menu's anchor), else the control the last main press landed on, while that press is recent: from its press until the next key press, the next focus change, or one second after the pointer came up.
  • Escape that the stack used. When escape asks a layer to close, or the screen's chain used the key, the host marks the key as handled (preventDefault() on the web), so older listeners on the page leave it alone. When nothing used it, the key goes on.
  • Tab in a menu. When tab returns requestClose(menu, 'tab'), the host consumes the key: focus does not move on, and goes back to the opener through restoreFocus when the menu closes. When tab returns nothing, the key moves focus as usual.
  • Confirm destructive. request when the user asks for the dangerous action, confirm for the dialog's confirm button, cancel{reason} for its Cancel button, Escape or the scrim, and the run's result.
  • List focus. setRows{rows} whenever the rows change, with the whole list (not only the rows a virtualised list has drawn). focusIn when focus enters the list. Arrow keys, Home and End as up, down, home, end. A printable character as type{char}, exactly one character. Space is type{char: " "} while the typeahead state is not empty, and activate otherwise. Enter is activate. A pointer press on a row is press{id}.
  • Load state. start when the screen opens or what it shows changes. refresh{byUser} for a refresh: byUser is true for a refresh button or pull to refresh, false for a refetch on focus or reconnect. retry for Try again.

docs.title: One dialog, two patterns
docs.text:
A confirm dialog is also a layer of the overlay stack. The host joins them:

  • An overlay requestClose(dialog, 'escape') or requestClose(dialog, 'scrim') becomes cancel{reason: 'escape'} or cancel{reason: 'scrim'} for the confirm pattern.
  • When the confirm pattern goes back to idle, the owner closes the dialog and reports closed to the overlay stack.
  • While the action runs, the confirm pattern ignores the cancel, so the owner does not close the dialog and reports nothing to the overlay stack.
  • requestClose(dialog, 'parentClosed') cannot be refused: the dialog has left the stack and is gone from the screen. Before the action and after a failure it is cancel. While the action runs, the run goes on. Its success is done as usual. Its failure has no dialog to show in, so the host sends cancel right after failed (the confirmation is closed again, and a later request opens it) and shows the message as a danger toast through notify. If the dialog comes back on the page before the result (its parent reopened), a failure shows in the dialog as usual, with no toast. The pattern does not cover this case yet; this is the host's rule.

docs.title: Toast queue
docs.text:
What the user sees. One toast at a time. If more arrive, they wait their turn. Each one leaves on its own after a while, or when the user dismisses it. While the pointer or focus is on a toast, or the window is hidden, or a dialog is open, it stays. A plain toast (no action, not a failure) that has waited too long for its turn is dropped; nothing is dropped while it could not be seen.

Rules:

  • One toast shows at a time. A toast shown while nothing is showing appears at once, starts its timer and is announced to screen readers.
  • A toast shown while another is showing waits at the end of the queue. It is not announced until it shows.
  • A toast with the same id as the one showing replaces it, and its timer starts again. It is announced again only if its message or action changed. Use this for a toast that changes, such as "Uploading" then "Uploaded".
  • A toast with the same id as a waiting toast replaces that one in its place.
  • At most three toasts wait. When a toast arrives at a full queue, the oldest waiting toast with no action that is not danger is dropped. If there is none, the oldest waiting toast that is not danger goes. The new toast and danger toasts are never dropped, so the queue can grow past three.
  • A neutral or positive toast stays for the toast timing; with an action, for the longer toastAction timing.
  • A danger toast interrupts screen readers. The others wait for a pause. A danger toast without an action leaves after the longer timing. A danger toast with an action stays until the user dismisses it, and the toasts behind it wait.
  • Dismissing the toast that is showing brings in the next one, or nothing.
  • Dismissing a waiting toast removes it. Dismissing a toast that is not there does nothing.
  • When the timer ends, the toast leaves.
  • While the host has a reason to pause, the timer stops. When the last reason ends, the timer starts again from the full time, not from the time that was left.
  • The pause belongs to the toast area, not to one toast. A toast that takes the place of a dismissed one while paused waits too.
  • Every announcement includes the action's label, so a screen reader user knows the action is there.
  • When the user dismisses a toast with focus inside the toast area, focus goes back to where it was before it entered the area.
  • A waiting toast with no action that is not danger is dropped once it has waited the toastAction timing (8 seconds): by then "Saved" or "Copied" is stale. A toast with an action (Undo) and a danger toast are never dropped: they wait however long it takes. The wait starts when the toast joins the queue. It does not count while the toast area is paused, whatever the reason (the pointer or focus on the toast, the window hidden, a dialog open): the pause stops every wait, and when it ends each one starts again from the full time. So nothing raised behind a dialog is dropped unseen: it shows, and is announced, after the dialog closes. A toast whose turn comes first shows for its full time, also when its turn and its wait's end come at the same moment. Replacing a waiting toast with the same id keeps its wait (a fresher "3 new messages" keeps the clock of "2 new messages"); if the replacement has an action or is danger, it is not dropped when the wait ends.

The toast area is a landmark region named "Notifications". Keyboard users reach it with F6, and F6 (or Shift+F6) inside it puts focus back where it was. While a dialog or sheet is open the area is out of reach and F6 does nothing.

Parameters: durationMs (toast), durationWithActionMs (toastAction), maxQueued (3), maxWaitMs (toastAction).

Example. "Saved" appears and starts a four-second timer. A danger toast, "Couldn't send", arrives and waits. After four seconds "Saved" leaves and "Couldn't send" appears, interrupts the screen reader, and stays eight seconds. Had it carried a "Retry" action, it would stay until dismissed, and a "Saved" arriving behind it would be dropped after waiting eight seconds.

Host checklist Done when Timers startTimer starts one keyed by token; cancelTimer stops it Announcements Message then action label, at the given politeness Pause One pause/resume pair for pointer, focus, hidden window and open modal; pause again when a new toast appears while a reason holds Dismiss focusInside sent; returnFocus puts focus back Reach The area is a landmark; F6 moves focus into it and back; nothing while a modal is open Waits A wait's startTimer runs like any other (the reducer cancels waits on pause). When a wait and the showing toast's timer end at the same moment, send the showing toast's timerFired first (the web host delivers an ended wait one task later) Ids Callers use one id per subject

docs.title: Overlay stack
docs.text:
What the user sees. Escape, and on Android the Back gesture or button, close the innermost thing first. A press outside a menu or popover closes it. A press on the dimmed page closes the dialog. When something closes and focus was in it, focus goes back where it came from.

The stack holds the layers above the screen: tooltips, menus, popovers, dialogs and sheets (see Which overlay). Each layer knows the layer that owns it, the element that opened it and the layer that element is in.

Rules:

  • Layers stack in the order they open. A tooltip always sits on top.
  • Opening a layer that is already open does nothing.
  • Escape asks the topmost layer to close. One Escape closes one layer, so nested layers close innermost first.
  • A tooltip takes the Escape. Escape with a tooltip showing closes only the tooltip. It does not close the dialog below, and it does not reach the screen. The tooltip stays hidden until the pointer or focus leaves its control and comes back (the host's job).
  • Escape with nothing open goes to the screen. The screen has its own order: close the docked panel, then mark as read.
  • Escape while an input method is composing text never reaches the stack. A focused control that uses Escape itself (an open mention list, a message in edit mode) gets it first.
  • A press inside a layer owned by another layer counts as inside both. A select list opened from a dialog is part of the dialog.
  • A press outside a popover closes it, and the press carries on to what is underneath.
  • A press outside a menu closes the menu and goes no further. The control under the press is not activated.
  • A press outside a dialog or sheet is a press on its dimmed page. It asks the dialog to close and goes no further.
  • A press never closes a tooltip. A tooltip closes when the pointer or focus leaves its control.
  • Tab closes a menu. In any other layer, Tab moves focus as usual.
  • Closing is a request. The owner may refuse it, for example a form with unsaved changes. A layer leaves only when its owner says it has closed.
  • When a layer closes, the layers it owns close with it, innermost first. That is a command: their owners must close them.
  • When a layer closes with focus inside it, or with focus lost, focus goes back to the element that opened it. If that has gone, focus goes to the layer that element was in. If that has gone too, the screen decides. If the user had already moved focus somewhere else, focus stays there.
  • Focus never goes back to something under an open dialog or sheet.
  • A layer opened from inside another layer that has since closed takes over that layer's opener. So a confirm dialog opened from a menu's Delete item returns focus to the menu's button.
  • Closing a tooltip does not move focus.
  • The system Back (Android's Back gesture or button) closes the topmost layer that is not a tooltip, one layer per Back, and closes any tooltip with it: a tooltip never takes the Back. The owner may refuse, as with Escape.
  • Back with no layer open goes back a screen, the platform's way. Back never runs the screen's Escape chain, so it never marks a channel as read.

Parameters: none.

Example. The user opens the More menu on a message and chooses Delete. The confirm dialog opens and the menu closes; focus stays in the dialog. The user presses Escape: the dialog closes and focus goes back to the More button.

Host checklist Done when Layers Every tooltip, menu, popover, dialog and sheet sends open and closed, with parent, opener and openerLayer Escape One handler sends escape with composing and focusOwnsEscape; a tooltip closed by Escape stays hidden until re-entered Presses pressOutside with the innermost layer; the swallowed press is not passed on Tab Consumed when it closes a menu Back The system Back sends back while a layer that is not a tooltip is open; passToPlatform goes back a screen Closing closed reports openerPresent and focus; parentClosed is always obeyed Focus restoreFocus focuses the element, the layer, or (null) the screen's focus target

Where it stands. On the web, the kit's Tooltip, Menu, Popover, Dialog, Sheet and SelectField list meet every row (frontend/src/kit/behaviour/hosts/overlay.ts), and each rule has a test that drives the real components (frontend/src/__tests__/kit/behaviour/hosts/overlay.test.tsx). The focus trap with layers inside a dialog, Escape during composition, a drag onto the dimmed page, the press a menu swallows, focus return when a click focuses nothing, and the live region inside the topmost layer run in real browsers (frontend/browser-tests/overlay-stack.spec.ts). The system Back runs in the Lounge on touch devices (frontend/src/kit/behaviour/hosts/systemBack.ts, tested in frontend/src/__tests__/kit/behaviour/hosts/systemBack.test.tsx and, on a phone-sized touch browser, frontend/e2e/lounge-back.spec.ts). The native client has no host yet.

Two things the web host does because of how MUI works, not because the pattern asks for them. A native host need not copy them:

  • A press during which a layer opened is not a press. MUI's select list opens when the pointer goes down, under the pointer, and would otherwise close as it comes up.
  • When a step asks child layers to close with parentClosed and also moves focus, focus moves once the children have gone: a closing MUI menu still holds focus inside itself until then.

docs.title: Confirm destructive
docs.text:
What the user sees. Before something that cannot be undone, a dialog asks "Are you sure?". While the action runs, the button shows it is busy and the dialog cannot be closed. If it fails, the dialog stays open with the error, and the user can try again or cancel.

Rules:

  • The dialog is closed until something asks for it. Asking again while it is open does nothing.
  • The confirm button starts the action.
  • While the action runs, pressing confirm again does nothing.
  • While the action runs, nothing closes the dialog: not Cancel, not Escape, not a press on the dimmed page. The action may already have happened.
  • Before the action, and after it fails, Cancel, Escape and a press on the dimmed page all close the dialog.
  • When the action succeeds, the dialog closes and the screen is told it is done.
  • When the action fails, the dialog stays open and shows the error.
  • Confirm after a failure tries again, and the error goes away while it runs.
  • A late answer from an earlier try is ignored.

Parameters: none.

Example. The user chooses Delete channel. The dialog asks. They press Delete: the button is busy. The server says no. The dialog shows "Couldn't delete the channel". They press Delete again; this time it works, and the dialog closes.

On the web. useConfirmDestructive({ title, description, confirmLabel, run, errorMessage?, timeoutMessage?, onDone?, timeoutMs? }) returns { request, dialog, phase }; request keeps its identity across renders. Wire request to the dangerous button or Menu item and render dialog once in the screen's tree. It is the kit Dialog (see ConfirmDialog in Components).

  • run(signal) has timeoutMs (30 seconds by default) to answer; a timeout is a failure. A screen that goes away while the action works counts as failed, and the late answer is dropped. Each run reports exactly one result. The signal aborts when the answer no longer counts: a timeout (its reason is a ConfirmTimeoutError) or the screen going away.
  • errorMessage(error) words a rejection. A timeout does not go through it: the result is unknown, so the dialog says "This is taking too long. It may still have worked, so check before you try again." (timeoutMessage replaces it). The confirm button stays, with its label, for a second try.
  • Cancel is aria-disabled while the action works: it reads as unavailable and ignores presses, but keeps focus (Safari leaves focus on it when the confirm button is clicked). A failure shows as a danger Alert in the body, and the confirm button keeps its label, so it reads as the retry.
  • Opened from a Menu item, the dialog's opener is the menu's button (rule 17 of the overlay stack), so focus goes back to it.
  • onDone runs after the dialog has closed and focus has gone back.
  • When the layer the dialog was opened from closes (a Sheet or Popover it was rendered in), the dialog goes with it, and the same happens when the dialog element leaves the page. Before the action and after a failure that is a cancel. While the action works, the dialog disappears but the action keeps running: success calls onDone; failure shows its message as a danger toast (the kit's toast host, the same queue as useToasts, with an id of its own per confirmation) and the hook goes back to idle, so request() opens the dialog again. If that layer reopens before the result, the dialog shows again and a failure appears in it as usual. See "One dialog, two patterns".
  • Rule: a dialog rendered inside a Popover, Sheet or other layer that can close while the action works reports a failure after that close only as a toast, so the screen must render the toast region: inside AppFrame it always does (AppFrame renders ToastRegion). Outside it (a story, a test), render <ToastRegion /> yourself, or the notice waits in the queue unseen.
Host checklist Done when Results Every run reports exactly one succeeded or failed, a timeout included Overlay Escape and scrim close requests become cancel; closed is reported when the phase goes back to idle Busy The confirm button is busy while working

docs.title: List focus
docs.text:
What the user sees. In a menu, a picker or a channel list, the arrow keys move between rows, Home and End jump to the ends, and typing letters jumps to a row. Disabled rows are skipped.

Rules:

  • Only enabled rows take focus. Disabled rows are skipped, in menus too; a disabled item that the user needs to discover should say why in its own text or not be shown.
  • In an empty list, or one where every row is disabled, keys do nothing.
  • Down moves to the next row and Up to the previous one. With nothing focused, Down goes to the first row and Up to the last.
  • At the ends, Down and Up stop. A list can choose to wrap round instead.
  • Home goes to the first row and End to the last.
  • Every time focus enters the list, it goes to the selected row; if nothing usable is selected, to the row focus last left; if there is none, to the first row. This never changes the selection.
  • Typing letters jumps to the first row whose label starts with them, from the focused row onwards and round. Case does not matter. The letters add up for one second (the typeahead timing), then start again.
  • Typing the same letter again steps through the rows that start with it.
  • If no row matches, focus stays where it is.
  • By default, moving focus does not select. Enter or Space selects the focused row.
  • A list can choose to select as focus moves, for example tabs in a tab list.
  • Clicking a row focuses and selects it. Clicking a disabled row does nothing.
  • When rows change and the focused row goes away or becomes disabled, focus moves to the next row, or the previous one if there is none. The selection moves with it only in a list that selects as focus moves.
  • When the selected row goes away, nothing is selected.
  • The screen can set the selection from outside the list, as a route or a value changes it (setSelected). That only moves the selection: nothing is chosen, no select is emitted, and focus and the typed letters stay where they are. An id that names no row means nothing is selected; once the row arrives, the host sets it again.
  • When focus leaves the list (focusOut), the typed letters are dropped and nothing else changes. Where focus comes back is decided when it enters, so a selection changed while the user was away is where they come back, whether it was set, cleared, removed or disabled meanwhile.
  • When a row gets focus some other way than the list's keys (a click, a screen reader, code, or focus landing on one of the row's own controls; focusRow), that row becomes the focused row, so the arrows go on from there. It never selects, also in a list that selects as focus moves: a tab is chosen by its click, Enter or Space, or an arrow key.
  • "Case does not matter" means each character is put in lower case on its own, the same way in every language (Python's str.lower() on one character at a time). Characters are then compared exactly, so an emoji only matches itself.

This pattern is for a single list with one selection. Multi-select lists and grids are future patterns.

Parameters: wrap (off), selectionFollowsFocus (off), typeaheadMs (typeahead).

Example. A list has General, Games and Random. The user types "g": focus goes to General. They type "g" again: Games. They type "r" after a pause: Random.

Host checklist Done when Rows setRows carries the whole list on every change Keys Arrows, Home, End, Enter; Space is type while the buffer is not empty Typeahead One character per type; the timer runs as the effects say Selection select and deselect acted on; the host reads focused to move real focus Selection from outside setSelected whenever the screen's selection differs from the pattern's, also after setRows Focus in and out focusOut when focus moves outside the list (not between its rows or to a row's controls); focusRow when a row gets focus that the host did not move there

The web host (useListFocus in frontend/src/kit/behaviour/hosts/listFocus.ts):

  • Roving tabindex: the list has one Tab stop, the focused row, or before the list is entered (and whenever focus is outside it) the row focus will enter on by the rule above, kept up to date as the selection and rows change. Real focus moves with focused, so screen readers and the focus ring follow it.
  • Keys: Up and Down in a vertical list; in a horizontal one (Tabs) Left and Right too. Home and End. Keys with Ctrl, Alt or Meta (AltGr letters still type), keys an IME is composing, keys a control already handled (defaultPrevented) and keys from anything that is not a row or a row's trailing control pass by. A letter is type when typeahead is on. A held Enter or Space chooses once.
  • Activation follows the browser's own click: Enter on a link or button, and Space on a button, click the row natively, and that click (detail 0) is activate. Space on a link would scroll the page, so the host presses the link itself. A pointer click is press. A modified click on a link (a new tab) is left to the browser; on a button row it still chooses the row. So a link navigates once and nothing is chosen twice.
  • Space on a row while letters are pending is type, and its keydown and keyup are both taken so the row is not pressed. On a trailing control, Space is that control's.
  • Focus never falls to the page: when the focused element in the list goes away (a row removed, a row's element replaced, a trailing control that unmounts), the host focuses its row, else the pattern's row. It checks after every render and on every change under the list. When focus is elsewhere, nothing in the list takes it.
  • reveal(id) runs before a row is focused, so a virtualised list can render it; the host focuses the row once it is rendered, however many frames that takes. A virtualised list keeps its Tab stop row (the focused or selected row) rendered, or Tab skips the list.
  • In a vertical list, a row's trailing controls are not Tab stops: Right goes from the row into them and Left back.
  • Focus leaving the list container (focusout to anything outside it, or to nothing) is focusOut. One capture-phase focus handler on the list sends, in order, focusIn when focus arrives from outside, then focusRow when the focus is on a row (or a row's trailing control) other than the pattern's focused row. Tab arrives on the Tab stop, which is rule 6's row, so it sends only focusIn; a click or a screen reader arriving on another row sends both. Neither moves or reveals anything: real focus is already where it is.

docs.title: Load state
docs.text:
What the user sees. A screen that loads from the server shows one of five things: a skeleton while it loads, the content, an empty state, an error with Try again, or the content while it refreshes. An error only takes over the screen when there is nothing else to show.

Rules:

  • A screen starts by loading.
  • Opening the screen, or changing what it shows (another channel, for example), loads from scratch. Whatever was shown goes.
  • Refreshing keeps the content on screen while it loads again.
  • Refreshing an empty screen keeps the empty state.
  • Refreshing after an error is the same as Try again.
  • Refreshing while a load is already running starts no new load. A refresh the user started still marks that load as theirs.
  • Try again on the error screen loads again. Anywhere else it does nothing.
  • When the load succeeds, the screen shows the content, or the empty state if there is nothing.
  • When the first load fails, the error screen replaces the skeleton.
  • When a refresh fails, the content stays and a toast says what went wrong. The toast has the same id every time for that screen, so repeated failures replace one toast instead of stacking.
  • A late answer from an earlier load is ignored.
  • While a refresh the user started is running, the control that started it (the refresh button) shows it is busy. A refresh in the background shows nothing.

Parameters: notifyId (the toast id for this screen's refresh failures; each screen sets its own).

Example. The member list loads and shows. The connection drops and the list refreshes in the background; the refresh fails. The members stay on screen, and a toast says "You are offline". It fails again a minute later: the same toast is replaced, not added.

On the web. useLoadState({ notifyId, resetKey, load, isEmpty }) takes a function that fetches: load(signal) returns the data, and the signal aborts when a newer fetch starts or the screen goes away. It returns { state, data }: state is the controller, and data is the current load's answer only, so a late answer for an earlier resetKey never shows, even when load ignores the signal. useQueryLoadState(query, { notifyId, resetKey, isEmpty }) takes a TanStack Query result instead and returns the controller (draw query.data). Both accept an optional errorMessage(error), shown under the screen's error title ("Couldn't load members"). Without one, the error screen shows the title and the Try again button and no body (the button is the next step; the words would only repeat it), and a refresh failure toasts "Couldn't refresh. Try again.". The controller (status, error, retryable, refreshByUser, refresh(), retry()) is what <LoadState> draws (see LoadState in Components).

  • resetKey is a string or a number, compared by value. Build it from ids (channelId, or `${communityId}:${channelId}`), never an array or an object, and change it in the same render as the query key. A change is start: the screen loads from scratch, and the answer to the earlier key is dropped.
  • resetKey is compared with Object.is; NaN (Number(missingId)) throws.
  • useQueryLoadState observes the query; it never fetches by itself. On open and on a resetKey change, data in the cache is the first face painted (ready or empty), with no skeleton and no request, whatever the query is doing: fresh, disabled, offline, or its last refetch failed. A refetch TanStack makes of that data on mount (it is stale) is a background refresh; offline, it fails into a toast, never the error screen. With no data, it joins the query's own fetch.
  • Only Try again and a refresh the user starts call refetch(), and only while the query is enabled and not fetching already. A disabled query with no answer (a dependent query whose id has not arrived, or one waiting on a permission) reads as loading, never empty or error, and fetches nothing; a cached error on a disabled query keeps the skeleton too, since Try again could not fetch it.
  • A refetch the query starts itself (focus, reconnect, invalidation) is a background refresh; one that ended before the screen saw it start, and data set by hand (setQueryData from a socket handler), are reported the same way and settle at once.
  • A cancelled fetch (cancelQueries, which reverts) is not a result. During the first load the skeleton stays, and the hook calls refetch() once to resume the load the cancel interrupted (once only: a second cancel is left alone). During a refresh the reverted data, or the data a socket handler sets right after, ends the refresh.
  • A paused fetch (offline: TanStack waits instead of failing) is a failed attempt. A first load shows the error face with "You're offline. It will load when you're back online." and no Try again (the controller's retryable is false): TanStack resumes the paused fetch on reconnect, so the screen loads by itself, and Try again would only fail again. A refresh notifies "You're offline. It will refresh when you're back online." and its button stops being busy. When the connection returns, the resumed fetch's answer shows as a background refresh.
  • notify goes straight to the kit's toast host (the queue behind useToasts): show({ id: notifyId, tone: 'danger', message }), so repeated failures replace one toast. The toast region AppFrame renders draws it.
Host checklist Done when Fetches Every fetch reports one result with its token Refresh byUser set right; busy shown on the control while refreshByUser Notify notify goes to the toast queue with its id; notifyId set per screen

docs.title: How to read a pattern file
docs.text:
Each pattern is a file in design/behaviour/, for example design/behaviour/toast-queue.json. It holds:

  • pattern and doc: the name and what the pattern is for.
  • params: the settings, with defaults. A duration names its timing token, such as motion.toast.
  • state: what the pattern remembers.
  • events: what can happen, and what each event carries.
  • effects: what the pattern can ask its host to do.
  • rules: the behaviour in plain sentences, numbered from 1.
  • scenarios: short stories, each a name and a list of events. covers says which rules a scenario shows. Every rule is covered by at least one scenario.

An event and an effect are written the same way: a name, then its fields. {"timerFired": {"token": 1}} is the event "the timer with token 1 fired".

docs.title: How to read a vector
docs.text:
The generator runs each scenario through the Python definition and writes the result to design/vectors/behaviour.json. That result is a vector. For each event it gives the full state after it, and the exact effects, in order.

For example, the first step of "second toast waits":

  • Event: show a toast "Saved".
  • State: "Saved" is showing, the queue is empty, timer token 1.
  • Effects: start timer 1 for 4000 ms, then announce "Saved", politely, with no action.

Nobody types the expected state by hand. Change a scenario or the definition, run the generator, and the vectors follow. The web and native reducers are then tested against them.

docs.title: Adding or changing a pattern
docs.text:
A pattern is part of the design system, so adding one, or changing a rule, is a decision for the project owner (see Extending the system and the three rules). Ask first. Do not change a pattern to suit one screen.

Once it is agreed:

  1. Change the rules and scenarios in the pattern file.
  2. Change the Python definition (design/gen/behaviour_ref.py) and its tests. Each rule has a test named for it.
  3. Run the generator: python3 design/gen/gen_tokens.py.
  4. Change the web and native reducers until they pass the new vectors.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The kit is the app's own set of components. The web client and the native client use the same names and the same options, so a screen built from the kit looks and behaves the same in both.

Screens are built only from kit components. Do not make a one-off button, field or label for a single screen. If you need something the kit does not cover, do not improvise: follow Extending the system. The kit's provider supplies the colours and fonts to everything inside it.

The live examples are the kit stories in frontend/src/stories/kit/. A story id is the file name plus the export name, in lower-case words joined by hyphens. The export States in KitButton.stories.tsx is kit-button--states. The stories show each component in dark, light and tinted colour, and in its states. Copy from them, not from a picture.

Fifty-two components exist so far: Text, Button, Icon, IconButton, KeyCap, Tabs, Switch, Checkbox, RadioGroup, Slider, TextField, SelectField, Avatar, AvatarStack, MediaTile, Badge, Pill, Spinner, LinearProgress, Skeleton, Alert, LoadState, Toast, ListRow, PickerGrid, Table, Menu, Popover, Tooltip, Dialog, ConfirmDialog, MediaViewer, Island, Card, Sheet, Dock, DockDivider, DockItem, Stack, CallStack, and the chat pieces MessageRow, MessageText, ListSeparator, ReactionChip, Composer, JumpToLatest, ChatPane, MessageQuote, AttachmentTile, LinkCard, TypingLine and SuggestionList.

The Android app's Compose kit (native/android/kit) has the pieces its first screens need, with the same names and options in Compose's style (enums for the variants, lambdas for the handlers, slots for leading and trailing): Text, Button, Icon, IconButton, TextField, ListRow, Avatar, Spinner, Alert, Island and Card. They take the touch values in Tokens and colour ("Touch density"). Their stories are in native/android/kit/src/test/.../stories/KitStories.kt (ids kit-text, kit-button, kit-icon-button, kit-text-field, kit-list-row, kit-avatar, kit-spinner, kit-alert, kit-surfaces and the sample screen kit-sign-in), and native/scripts/android-ui-review.sh renders them. On Android, Avatar shows initials only for now (pictures come with the authenticated file fetch), and Button and IconButton leave out the web's aria-disabled, onUnavailablePress, current and hold.

docs.title: Rules every component follows
docs.text:
• Props are a closed list. A component takes only the variants and sizes listed for it. There is no per-use styling: no custom colour, width or padding. If none of the listed options fits, the system needs extending.
  • Every interactive control has a label. The label may be hidden from the eye (labelHidden, or the label of an icon button), but it is never missing. Screen readers and keyboard users depend on it.
  • Hover only on devices that hover. A touch screen never shows a stuck hover. Pressed and keyboard focus always show.
  • Disabled takes a control out of the tab order and dims it.
  • Loading is not disabled. A busy control stays focusable and reachable by keyboard. It tells assistive technology that it is busy, and it ignores clicks and Enter. Use loading for work in progress. Use disabled only when the action is not available. If both are set, disabled wins: the control is disabled and shows no spinner.
  • Motion is small and optional. Animations only fade or move, use the timing tokens, and stop for people who ask their system for reduced motion.
  • Colours and sizes come only from the tokens and palette roles described in Tokens and colour.

docs.title: How a screen is built
docs.text:
The ground is the page. Islands float on the ground and hold everything: a screen is a few islands and nothing outside them. Inside an island go rows, cards, text and controls. Overlays float above everything, and they are the only thing that does.

Layer What it is Palette role Ground The page behind everything ground Island A large rounded panel that floats on the ground surface Card A soft block inside an island fill Overlay A Dialog, a Sheet or another floating panel surface, with a border and a shadow

The gap between islands belongs to the layout, not to the island. See Tokens and colour for the palette roles. The layout templates that arrange islands into a screen are in Layouts.

Kit pieces know which layer they sit on and adjust their own colours, so a designer never picks a different colour for a button because it is on a card. A soft Button on the ground or an island is fill; on a Card (itself fill) it is surface; inside a Dialog opened from that Card it is fill again, because an overlay panel is its own layer. A selected ListRow is the accent layer, and the pieces in it switch to the colours that read on the accent.

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
All words on a screen that are not inside another component. It sets the type style and the colour role of the words.

Use it when you show a title, a name, body copy, a small note or a tag.

Do not use it when the words are the label of a control. Pass them to that control as its label. Do not use it to make a link or a button. Use a Button with the text variant.

Prop Values Default Meaning variant title, section, name, body, bodyStrong, meta, small, tag body The type style. The sizes are in the Tokens and colour chapter. tone default, secondary, dim, accent, danger default The colour role of the words. as span, p, div, label, h1 to h6 none The page element, for structure. It does not change the look. truncate true, false false Cuts long text to one line with an ellipsis.

Stories: kit-text--variants, kit-text--tones, kit-text--truncated, kit-text--variants-light, kit-text--tones-tinted.

docs.title: Button
docs.text:
A control with a text label that starts an action.

Use it when the user does something: save, send, join, delete.

Do not use it when the control shows only an icon. Use IconButton. Do not use it to switch between views or modes. Use Tabs. Do not use it to turn a setting on or off. Use Switch.

Prop Values Default Meaning variant primary, soft, ghost, danger, quietDanger, text soft How loud the button is. See the guide below. size sm, md, lg md The size of the button. startIcon an icon none An icon before the label. fullWidth true, false false Stretches the button to the width of its space. loading true, false false The button is busy. See the rules above. disabled true, false false The action is not available. aria-disabled true, false false Not available right now, but still focusable: it reads as unavailable, looks dimmed and ignores clicks. Use it when focus may already sit on the button (Cancel while a ConfirmDialog works). type button, submit button Use submit for the button that sends a form.

A small button (sm) keeps its look but, on a touch screen (a coarse pointer), its hit area reaches the touch minimum (control.md), as a small IconButton's does. Web kit only so far.

docs.title: Which variant
docs.text:
• primary: the one main action on a surface. Use one per surface.
  • soft: ordinary actions.
  • ghost: low-emphasis actions in toolbars and rows.
  • danger: a destructive action that is the main action of a confirmation.
  • quietDanger: a destructive action that sits among other actions.
  • text: an inline action that reads like a link.

Stories: kit-button--variants, kit-button--states, kit-button--long-label, kit-button--focused, kit-button--focused-ghost, kit-button--focused-danger, kit-button--variants-light, kit-button--variants-tinted.

docs.title: Icon
docs.text:
A small picture from the app's icon set. It is for looking at, not pressing.

Use it when an icon sits beside text or on its own as a plain symbol.

Do not use it when the user can press it. Use IconButton. Do not draw an icon that is not in the set. Ask for it to be added.

Prop Values Default Meaning name a name from the icon set none (required) Which icon. size xs, sm, md, lg, xl md 14, 16, 18, 20 or 24 pixels. tone inherit, default, secondary, dim, accent, danger, positive, warning inherit The colour role. inherit takes the colour of the text around it. label text none Names the icon. Give one when the icon alone carries meaning. Without one it is decoration.

Stories: kit-icon--all, kit-icon--sizes, kit-icon--tones, kit-icon--all-light.

docs.title: IconButton
docs.text:
A button that shows only an icon.

Use it when the action is well known from its icon and space is tight, such as a toolbar or a row of actions.

Do not use it when the action needs words to be understood. Use Button.

It always needs a label. The label is not shown. It names the button for screen readers.

Prop Values Default Meaning icon a name from the icon set none (required) Which icon. label text none (required) The accessible name. variant ghost, soft, primary, danger ghost The same looks as the Button variants of those names. size sm, md, lg md The size of the button. selected true, false not set Marks a toggle as on. It fills the button and gives the icon the accent colour. loading true, false false The button is busy. See the rules above. disabled true, false false The action is not available. focus rowFocus(id) from useListFocus none Joins a keyboard list: today the Dock's. The button is then one stop of the list's single Tab stop. A disabled button ignores it. See Dock. aria-disabled true, false false Not available right now, but still a Tab stop with its name, as Button's: it reads as unavailable, looks dimmed, and a press does not run onClick or start a hold. Use it when the user must be able to find out why (the call bar's mic while a moderator has muted you), and say why with onUnavailablePress and a visible line. disabled and loading win over it. Web kit only so far. onUnavailablePress a function none Called instead of onClick when an aria-disabled button is pressed (a click, Enter or Space): say why it cannot act, with useAnnounce. Web kit only so far. badge a number none A count over the button's corner, the same danger Badge a DockItem shows (the Dock's Inbox). 0, or a number that is not finite, shows nothing. The count is added to the name: "Inbox, 9 unread". badgeMeaning unread, mentions unread What badge counts, in the name: "9 unread", or "1 mention" / "2 mentions". current true, false false The place you are in, for an item on the Dock: the accent ring a current DockItem has (a surface gap, then the accent), ", current" in the name before the count, and aria-current="page". Not a toggle: use selected for that. With keyboard focus the focus ring moves outside the current ring (its usual offset, past the ring), so the two never overlap. Web kit only so far. hold { onStart, onEnd } none Makes it a press-and-hold control (hold to talk). See below.

Press and hold. With hold the button is held, not clicked: onStart runs when a finger, pen or the main mouse button goes down on it, and onEnd runs exactly once when that hold ends. The pointer is captured, so sliding off the button keeps the hold, and lifting it anywhere ends it. Only the pointer that started the hold ends it: a second finger tapping the button neither starts another hold nor ends this one. The hold also ends when the pointer is cancelled (a call, the system taking the gesture), when capture is lost, when the button becomes disabled or stops being a hold control, and when it unmounts, so nothing is left held with no finger on it. The button does not scroll the page, select text or open the long-press menu. It has no pressed state of its own: show a hold that is running with variant (the call bar uses primary while it transmits). Keys do not hold it. Use it only where holding is the action (hold to talk); for anything else use a plain button.

Web kit only so far; the native kit has not caught up (see Extending the system).

Stories: kit-icon-button--variants, kit-icon-button--states, kit-icon-button--focused, kit-icon-button--variants-light, kit-icon-button--variants-tinted, kit-icon-button--badge-and-current, kit-icon-button--badge-and-current-light, kit-icon-button--badge-and-current-tinted, kit-icon-button--current-focused, kit-icon-button--current-focused-light, kit-icon-button--current-focused-tinted, kit-icon-button--hold, kit-icon-button--hold-light, kit-icon-button--unavailable, kit-icon-button--unavailable-light.

docs.title: KeyCap
docs.text:
A small key shape that shows one keyboard key, such as a shortcut hint.

Use it when you tell the user which key to press.

Do not use it when the text is not a key. Use Text.

It takes one string as its content and has no options.

Stories: kit-key-cap--keys, kit-key-cap--keys-light.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
A row of choices where exactly one is selected.

Use it when the user picks one of a few views or options, and the choice stays visible.

Do not use it when the choice is a setting to turn on or off (use Switch), one option out of a form that needs descriptions (use RadioGroup), or a long list of options (use SelectField).

Each tab has an id, a label, and optionally a count, disabled and panelId. The label prop names the whole row for screen readers. A tab with a count is named "Mentions, 3" for screen readers; the eye sees the label and the count as they are drawn. Clicking the tab that is already selected does nothing.

To link a tab to the panel it controls, give the tab a panelId (it becomes aria-controls) and label the panel by the tab: every tab gets the id <list id>-tab-<tab id>, and tabElementId(listId, tabId) returns it. Pass your own id to Tabs so the screen can build the panel's aria-labelledby with that helper. Without an id, Tabs makes one of its own, and the tab ids are still unique on the page.

Prop Values Default Meaning variant underline, segmented underline The look. See below. fullWidth true, false false Spreads the tabs across the width of their space. value a tab id none (required) The selected tab. id text made for you The id of the row. Also the start of every tab's id.

A row that is wider than its space scrolls inside it, with a thin scrollbar, and starts scrolled so the selected tab is visible, also when value changes from outside. Tabs takes no ref.

Keys come from the list focus pattern (Behaviour): the row is one Tab stop (the selected tab), Left and Right and also Up and Down move to the next or previous tab and select it, wrapping round, Home and End go to the ends, and disabled tabs are skipped. There is no typeahead. When focus comes back to the row, it lands on the selected tab, also if value changed while focus was elsewhere. Tabbing in never changes the tab, and a tab is chosen on click, not when the pointer goes down.

docs.title: Underline or segmented
docs.text:
• underline: switch between views of a page, such as the sections of a settings screen.
  • segmented: filter or switch mode within one view. Keep it to a few short options.

Stories: kit-tabs--underline, kit-tabs--segmented, kit-tabs--with-counts, kit-tabs--overflow, kit-tabs--last-tab-selected, kit-tabs--segmented-focused, kit-tabs--segmented-focused-light, kit-tabs--segmented-light, kit-tabs--segmented-tinted.

docs.title: Switch
docs.text:
A control that turns one setting on or off at once.

Use it when the change takes effect immediately, such as muting a sound.

Do not use it when the choice is part of a form that is saved later, or when the user may choose several items from a list. Use Checkbox.

Prop Values Default Meaning checked true, false none (required) On or off. label text none (required) The name of the setting. description text none A line of help under the label. labelHidden true, false false Hides the text from the eye. It still names the switch. disabled true, false false The setting is not available.

Stories: kit-switch--states, kit-switch--focused, kit-switch--long-label, kit-switch--switch-light, kit-switch--switch-tinted.

docs.title: Checkbox
docs.text:
A box the user ticks to include or exclude an item.

Use it when the user picks any number of items from a list, or agrees to something in a form.

Do not use it when the change takes effect at once (use Switch) or when exactly one option must be chosen (use RadioGroup).

Prop Values Default Meaning checked true, false none (required) Ticked or not. indeterminate true, false false Shows a dash (the Minus icon) for a parent whose children are only partly ticked. The dash stays for as long as you pass true, also after a click: your onChange decides what happens next. label text none (required) The name of the choice. description text none A line of help under the label. labelHidden true, false false Hides the text from the eye. It still names the checkbox. disabled true, false false The choice is not available.

Stories: kit-checkbox--states, kit-checkbox--focused, kit-checkbox--long-label, kit-checkbox--checkbox-light, kit-checkbox--checkbox-tinted.

docs.title: RadioGroup
docs.text:
A set of options where exactly one is chosen.

Use it when there are a few options and the user should see them all at once, perhaps each with a description.

Do not use it when there are many options (use SelectField), when the options are views of a page or a filter (use Tabs), or when the choice is a single on or off (use Switch or Checkbox).

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) Names the group. Shown above the options unless labelHidden. labelHidden true, false false Hides the group label from the eye. It still names the group. options a list of value, label, and optionally description and disabled none (required) The choices. orientation vertical, horizontal vertical How the options are laid out. disabled true, false false The whole group is not available.

Stories: kit-radio-group--states, kit-radio-group--focused, kit-radio-group--long-label, kit-radio-group--radio-group-light, kit-radio-group--radio-group-tinted.

docs.title: Slider
docs.text:
A control for choosing a number in a range by dragging.

Use it when the exact number matters less than the feel, such as a volume.

Do not use it when the user must type an exact value. Number entry will be its own component; TextField takes text only.

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) Names the slider. Shown above it unless labelHidden. min, max numbers 0 and 100 The ends of the range. step a number 1 The size of one step. Values snap to the grid of steps counted from min, so a step of 0.1 gives 0.3 and not 0.30000000000000004. formatValue a function from number to text none Turns the value into the text shown beside the label, for example "80%". It is also what screen readers read. labelHidden true, false false Hides the label row from the eye. It still names the slider. disabled true, false false The slider is not available. ref a ref to an input element none Reaches the slider's input, so a form can focus it.

The label uses the same style as the labels of fields.

Stories: kit-slider--states, kit-slider--focused, kit-slider--focused-at-min, kit-slider--focused-at-max, kit-slider--formatted, kit-slider--long-label, kit-slider--slider-light, kit-slider--slider-tinted.

docs.title: TextField
docs.text:
A field where the user types text, on one line or on several.

Use it when the user enters a name, a message, a search, a password or any free text.

Do not use it when the answer is one of a fixed list. Use SelectField or RadioGroup.

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) Names the field. Shown above it unless labelHidden. placeholder text none A hint inside the empty field. It does not replace the label. helper text none A line of help under the field. error text none An error message. It marks the field invalid and replaces the helper. required true, false false Marks the field as required. disabled true, false false The field is not available. labelHidden true, false false Hides the label from the eye. It still names the field. shape field, round field field is the standard shape. round is the fully rounded shape. type text, password, email, search, url text The kind of text. Numbers have no type here: number entry will be its own component. multiline, rows true, false; a number false Makes the field several lines tall. startIcon a name from the icon set none An icon at the start of the field.

A multiline field without rows starts three rows tall and grows with its text; one with rows={1} is as tall as a single-line field. The error message is not a live region: an error that appears after a submit is read out when the field gets focus again, not when it appears. Move focus to the first invalid field after a failed submit.

Stories: kit-text-field--states, kit-text-field--shapes, kit-text-field--multiline, kit-text-field--narrow, kit-text-field--states-light, kit-text-field--states-tinted.

docs.title: SelectField
docs.text:
A field where the user picks one option from a list that opens on demand.

Use it when there are more options than fit on the screen, or the field sits in a form beside other fields.

Do not use it when there are only a few options and they should all be visible (use RadioGroup), or when the choice switches a view (use Tabs).

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) Names the field. Shown above it unless labelHidden. options a list of value, label, and optionally disabled none (required) The choices. placeholder text none Shown while the value matches no option. helper text none A line of help under the field. error text none An error message. It marks the field invalid and replaces the helper. disabled true, false false The field is not available. labelHidden true, false false Hides the label from the eye. It still names the field. ref a ref to an element none Receives the combobox element, so a form can focus the first invalid field.

Clicking the label focuses the field without opening the list, as a native select does. A value that matches no option shows the placeholder, and in development MUI logs a warning about it; pass a value from options or an empty string. The list's shadow is lighter in light mode than in dark mode.

Stories: kit-select-field--states, kit-select-field--open, kit-select-field--open-light, kit-select-field--long-options, kit-select-field--select-field-light, kit-select-field--select-field-tinted.

docs.title: Avatar
docs.text:
A person's or community's picture. When there is no picture, it shows their initials.

Use it when you show who someone is, or which community something belongs to, beside a name, a message or a row.

Do not use it when the picture is a plain symbol. Use Icon. Do not use it for a group of people. Use AvatarStack.

A person's or community's own colour is the one colour in the system that comes from data, not from the palette. The app may show it a little lighter or darker than they chose, so that the initials stay readable. People are circles. Communities are rounded squares. If the picture is missing or fails to load, the initials stay in its place and the layout does not move. A blank name gives a person icon.

Presence is shown by a small dot at the bottom right, and each state has its own shape as well as its own colour. online is a filled green dot. away is a filled amber dot with a bar across it. offline is a hollow grey ring. For speaking the whole avatar gets a green ring. The state is always also in the accessible name, for example "Ana Ruiz, away".

When the picture has loaded, the initials are no longer painted, so a logo with a transparent background shows no letters through it. The community colour still shows behind such a logo. Before the picture loads, and when it fails, the initials show. Punctuation and symbols at the start of a name are skipped, so "(mike)" gives "MI".

Prop Values Default Meaning name text none (required) Who it is. It is the accessible name and the source of the initials. src an image address none The picture, shown over the initials. colour a colour as #rrggbb none The person's or community's own colour. Without it the avatar uses the neutral fill. For a person, pass personColour(their user id). size xs, sm, md, lg, xl md 20, 28, 36, 44 or 64 pixels. See Avatar sizes in the Tokens and colour chapter. shape circle, rounded circle circle for people, rounded for communities. presence online, away, offline, speaking none The dot or ring, and the state in the accessible name. decorative true, false false Hides the avatar from screen readers. Use it only when the person's name is written right beside it.

A person's Avatar in a screen always gets colour={personColour(id)}, with their user id, so everyone keeps one colour on every screen and in both clients (see People colours in the Tokens and colour chapter). A person with no id and a webhook keep the neutral fill.

Stories: kit-avatar--sizes, kit-avatar--presence, kit-avatar--communities, kit-avatar--fallbacks, kit-avatar--transparent-image, kit-avatar--sizes-light, kit-avatar--presence-tinted, kit-avatar--people-colours, kit-avatar--people-colours-light, kit-avatar--people-colours-tinted.

docs.title: AvatarStack
docs.text:
A few avatars overlapping in a row, with the rest counted as "+N".

Use it when you show who is in a group, such as the people in a voice channel or the members of a conversation, in a small space.

Do not use it when each person needs to be read or pressed on their own. Use a list of rows with an Avatar each.

The stack is named as a whole, for example "Ana, Ben and 2 more". It is one image to a screen reader, and the avatars inside it are decorative. A blank name is read as "Unknown user". A stack with no people shows nothing.

A person who is talking (speaking) wears the same green ring as an Avatar with presence="speaking", and the name says so after the names: "pri, dropbear and aiko, dropbear is talking", or "pri and dropbear are talking" for two or more. The name counts everyone who is talking, also someone behind the "+N", who has no ring to show. More than three speakers are "A, B and 4 more are talking". A label replaces the whole name, so it must say who is talking itself. A speaking avatar does not overlap its neighbours: it and the avatar after it sit a ring's width apart, so the ring is whole and covers no one's initials; the stack is its own stacking context, so it never paints over anything outside it. (Avatar and MediaTile say ", speaking" in their names; the stack says "is talking" because it names a group.)

Prop Values Default Meaning people a list of name, and optionally src, colour and speaking none (required) Who is in the group. speaking draws the speaking ring on that avatar and adds them to the name. max a number 3 How many avatars to show before the "+N". size xs, sm, md, lg, xl sm The size of each avatar. label text the shown names and "and N more" The accessible name of the group.

Stories: kit-avatar--stack, kit-avatar--stack-speaking, kit-avatar--stack-speaking-light, kit-avatar--stack-speaking-tinted.

docs.title: MediaTile
docs.text:
A 16:9 rounded box for one participant's video, a shared screen, or, when they have no video, their avatar.

Use it when you show a video call's picture of one person or one shared screen: the call surface, the voice room.

Do not use it when you show a person in a list (use ListRow with an Avatar) or a small round picture (use Avatar). It draws no controls: put buttons beside it, not in it.

The tile is one group named by its label, with ", speaking" added while speaking is on; the ring is the same green ring Avatar uses for speaking, so the state is in the name as well as the colour. The tile has no video of its own: give it videoRef and it renders a muted, inline, auto-playing <video> that fills the tile (a screen is shown whole, a camera fills the box), and the label moves to a chip at the bottom left, so it reads on any picture. Without videoRef, or for avatar, the label is centred, with a large Avatar above it for avatar. A long label is cut with an ellipsis. The box is always 16:9 and as wide as its container; the container sets the size. A blank label reads "Unknown user".

Attaching a video. videoRef is a callback ref, not a ref object. The <video> element is drawn only while videoRef is set and kind is not avatar, and a new element is made whenever that changes (and when the tile remounts, for example when a keyed grid reorders). So attach the stream in the callback and detach on null:

const shown = useRef<HTMLVideoElement | null>(null);
const attach = useCallback(
  (element: HTMLVideoElement | null) => {
    if (element !== null) track.attach(element); // or element.srcObject = stream
    else if (shown.current !== null) track.detach(shown.current);
    shown.current = element;
  },
  [track],
);
<MediaTile kind="camera" label="pri" videoRef={track ? attach : undefined} />

Pass videoRef only while the track is live. When the track ends, or the person turns the camera off, pass undefined (and, for a camera, change kind to avatar): the tile falls back to the label or the avatar and the callback gets null. When kind changes between screen and camera the same element stays and its object-fit changes. Until the first frame the tile shows only its fill and the chip.

Small tiles. The tile measures its own width (a container query, widths from the avatar, spacing and text tokens). An avatar tile below about 203 px steps the avatar from xl to lg, below about 168 px it also takes the smaller padding (md avatar from about 139 px), and below that the name under the avatar goes: it is still the group's name. Nothing is cut off at any width, so two tiles side by side on a phone are fine.

Room for the ring. The speaking ring is drawn outside the box by two border.selected. A container that clips (overflow hidden or auto) must leave that much room around the tile, or the ring is cut at the edges.

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) Whose tile or what it shows. The accessible name, the caption and the source of an avatar tile's initials. kind screen, camera, avatar none (required) What the tile is. avatar never draws a video. speaking true, false false The speaking ring, and ", speaking" in the name. videoRef a callback (element: HTMLVideoElement or null) => void none Draws a <video> for screen and camera and hands it to you; called with null when it goes. See above.

Stories: kit-media-tile--kinds, kit-media-tile--kinds-light, kit-media-tile--kinds-tinted, kit-media-tile--speaking, kit-media-tile--speaking-light, kit-media-tile--long-label, kit-media-tile--small-tiles, kit-media-tile--small-tiles-light, kit-media-tile--phone-pair.

Web kit only so far; the native kit has not caught up (see Extending the system).

docs.title: Badge
docs.text:
A count, or a dot, attached to something else.

Use it when you show how many unread messages, mentions or requests an item has, or that something needs attention.

Do not use it when you name a state or a category in words. Use Pill. A Badge is not clickable. Put it on an item that is.

A count of 0 shows nothing. A count above max reads "99+". The number alone does not say what it counts, so a Badge always has a label, such as "3 unread".

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) What it means. It is the accessible name. count a number none The number to show. max a number 99 The largest number shown. Above it the badge reads, for example, "99+". dot true, false false A small dot with no number. It shows even when there is no count. tone accent, danger danger The colour role.

Stories: kit-badge--counts, kit-badge--counts-light, kit-badge--counts-tinted.

docs.title: Pill
docs.text:
A short word that names a state or a category.

Use it when you label a role, a status or the selected item: "Admin", "Live", "Muted".

Do not use it when you show a count. Use Badge. Do not use it as a button or a filter. A Pill is not clickable. Use Button, or Tabs for filters. Keep the text to a word or two.

The text always carries the meaning. The dot or icon is decoration. A tone other than accent colours the text on the neutral fill, so the word stays readable.

Prop Values Default Meaning children text none (required) The word. tone neutral, accent, danger, positive, warning neutral The colour role. dot true, false false A dot before the text, in the colour of the tone. icon a name from the icon set none An icon before the text. size sm, md md The size of the pill.

Stories: kit-pill--tones, kit-pill--tones-light, kit-pill--tones-tinted.

docs.title: Spinner
docs.text:
A small turning ring that shows something is working.

Use it when a short wait happens inside a control or a small panel, such as a button that is busy. For a button, use its loading option, which uses a Spinner for you.

Do not use it when content is loading in place and you know its shape. Use Skeleton. Do not use it when the wait spans a region or has a known length. Use LinearProgress.

It takes the colour of the text around it. The ring is a fixed arc that turns; it does not grow and shrink, and it stops under reduced motion. Without a label it is decoration and is hidden from screen readers. Give a label when the spinner is the only sign that something is busy.

Prop Values Default Meaning size xs, sm, md, lg, xl sm The same sizes as Icon. label text none Names the busy state for screen readers.

Stories: kit-spinner--sizes.

docs.title: LinearProgress
docs.text:
A thin bar that shows a wait across a region, such as an upload or a page.

Use it when the wait spans a region. Give it a value when you know how far along it is. Leave the value out when you do not, and the bar slides.

Do not use it when the wait is short and sits inside a control. Use Spinner. Do not use it when content is loading in place. Use Skeleton.

It always has a label that says what is in progress. A value outside 0 to 100 is held to that range. The bar keeps rounded ends at every value. Under reduced motion the sliding bar becomes a full, dimmed bar, which reads as "busy" and not as a number.

Prop Values Default Meaning label text none (required) What is in progress. It is the accessible name. value 0 to 100 none How far along it is. Without it the bar has no known length. tone accent, positive, danger accent The colour role of the bar.

Stories: kit-linear-progress--values, kit-linear-progress--values-light, kit-linear-progress--values-tinted.

docs.title: Skeleton
docs.text:
A grey placeholder in the shape of content that is still loading.

Use it when content is loading in place and you know its shape: lines of text, a round picture, a block.

Do not use it when the shape is not known, or the wait is inside a control. Use Spinner. Do not use it for a wait that spans a region. Use LinearProgress.

A Skeleton is hidden from screen readers. Name the loading state somewhere else on the screen, for example with a Spinner that has a label. The shape decides which other option applies.

Prop Values Default Meaning shape text, circle, rect none (required) The shape of the placeholder. lines a number 1 For text: how many lines, from 1 to 20 (anything else is held to that range). Each line is as tall as a line of body text. size xs, sm, md, lg, xl md For circle: the same sizes as Avatar. height sm, md, lg lg For rect: the same heights as a control, 32, 40 or 48 pixels.

Stories: kit-skeleton--shapes, kit-skeleton--shapes-light.

docs.title: Alert
docs.text:
A message that belongs to a place on the page.

Use it when you tell the user something about the screen they are on, and it should stay until the situation changes or they dismiss it: a connection problem, a warning above a form, a note about a setting.

Do not use it when the message is about something that just happened and can pass. Use Toast. Do not use it for an error on one field. Use the error of that field.

Prop Values Default Meaning severity info, success, warning, danger none (required) What kind of message. It sets the icon and its colour. title text none A bold first line. children text or content none (required) The message. action a label and an onClick none One action, shown as a text button under the message. secondaryAction a label and an onClick none A second text button beside action (Join and Decline on an incoming call). It is a choice, not a dismiss: dismissing is onClose. The buttons wrap onto a second line when they do not fit. onClose a function none Adds a Dismiss button. Without it the alert cannot be dismissed. announce true, false true Whether screen readers speak it when it appears. oneLine true, false false One line, for the banner row while a phone's on-screen keyboard is up: the title and the text run together and are cut with an ellipsis; the actions and Dismiss stay beside them. The whole text stays in the alert for screen readers. Web kit only so far.

warning and danger interrupt screen readers when they appear. info and success wait for a pause. Screen readers speak a live message when it shows up, so a banner that is already on the page when it loads would be read out on every visit. For those, pass announce={false}: the alert becomes a quiet note. Leave it on for an alert that appears because something happened.

Stories: kit-alert--severities, kit-alert--severities-light, kit-alert--severities-tinted, kit-alert--with-actions, kit-alert--long-text, kit-alert--secondary-action, kit-alert--secondary-action-light, kit-alert--secondary-action-long, kit-alert--secondary-action-one-long, kit-alert--one-line, kit-alert--one-line-light.

docs.title: LoadState
docs.text:
What a screen shows while it loads from the server: a skeleton, the content, an empty state, an error, or the content while it refreshes.

Use it when a region of a screen fetches its data and has to show all of those faces. Pass it the controller from useLoadState or useQueryLoadState (see Behaviour).

Do not use it when the wait is inside a control (a button's own loading), or when the content has no empty or error face worth drawing.

Prop Values Default Meaning state the controller from useLoadState or useQueryLoadState none (required) Which face to show, and what Try again calls. label text none (required) Names the region: "Members" reads "Loading members". skeleton content none (required) Skeletons in the shape of the content. empty content none (required) What shows when there is nothing to show. errorTitle text none (required) The first line of the error: "Couldn't load members". children content none (required) The content, shown when ready and while refreshing.
  • Loading: the skeleton and aria-busy on the region. A visually hidden status reads "Loading members". It sits outside the busy region (a screen reader may hold back changes inside one), is on the page on every face, and gets its text one commit after it mounts, so it is announced. The Skeleton itself is hidden from screen readers.
  • The region is a group named by label, focusable by script only (tabIndex={-1}). Try again moves focus to it as the button goes, so focus does not fall to the page, but only if focus is still on the page body then: focus the user moved elsewhere stays. It shows the kit focus ring on :focus-visible (after a keyboard Try again), none after a pointer press.
  • The error face offers Try again only when state.retryable (an offline first load has none: it loads by itself when the connection returns).
  • Error: a danger Alert with errorTitle and a Try again button, and the controller's message as its body when there is one (a screen's errorMessage, or the offline text). The default failure has no body: the title says what failed and the button what to do. It only shows when there is nothing else to show.
  • Refreshing: the content stays, with aria-busy. The refresh button reads state.refreshByUser for its own loading, so only a refresh the user started shows busy.
  • A failed refresh does not replace the content. The toast host shows it.

Stories: kit-load-state--loading, kit-load-state--loading-light, kit-load-state--ready, kit-load-state--empty, kit-load-state--empty-light, kit-load-state--error-with-retry, kit-load-state--error-with-retry-light, kit-load-state--error-with-message, kit-load-state--refreshing, kit-load-state--user-refresh-busy, kit-load-state--user-refresh-busy-light, kit-load-state--error-offline, kit-load-state--live, kit-load-state--refresh-fails-toast.

docs.title: Toast
docs.text:
A passing notice about something that just happened.

Use it when you confirm or report the result of an action: "Message sent", "Could not save".

Do not use it when the message belongs to a place on the page or must stay until the user acts. Use Alert.

A Toast is only the look of one notice. How long toasts stay and how they queue belong to the Behaviour chapter.

A danger toast interrupts screen readers when it appears. The others wait for a pause. announce={false} makes a toast a quiet note, for one that is already on the page at load.

Screens never render a Toast. They call useToasts() from the kit, from event handlers and effects (never while rendering): show({ id, tone, message, action }) returns the toast's id, and dismiss(id) takes it away. action is { label, onAction }; pressing it dismisses the toast and then runs onAction, so a follow-up shown under the same id (Retry failing again) stays. An action that throws or rejects is reported and the queue carries on. Use one id per subject ('offline', `upload-${fileId}`), so a second report replaces the first. AppFrame renders the toast region where Layouts says, and the host announces each toast, so the region's Toast is quiet. A screen's bottom-pinned element (the composer) calls useToastClearance(ref) so toasts sit above it. Rendering Toast directly is for the kit and its stories.

Prop Values Default Meaning message text none (required) What happened. tone neutral, positive, danger neutral The colour role. positive and danger add an icon. action a label and an onClick none One action, shown as a text button, such as "Undo". onClose a function none Adds a Dismiss button. announce true, false true Whether screen readers speak it when it appears.

Stories: kit-toast--tones, kit-toast--tones-light, kit-toast--tones-tinted, kit-toast--long-message; the region on the templates: kit-toast-region--in-call and the others listed in Layouts.

docs.title: ListRow
docs.text:
One row in a list of channels, people or places. It is the row of every list the user can move through or pick from.

Use it when you show a list of things the user opens, picks or just reads: channels, direct messages, members, settings pages.

Do not use it when you compare records by column (use Table), or when the row is a free-form card with its own layout.

A row takes one of three forms, set by what you pass it:

  • A link, when it goes somewhere. Pass href.
  • A button, when it does something. Pass onClick.
  • Plain, when it only shows information. Pass neither.

The whole row is the hit area of a link or a button: a press on the padding or the gap beside the text counts too, and so does the pointer cursor. trailing sits beside the link or button, not inside it, so it may hold buttons of its own. It sits above the row's hit area, so a press on one of those buttons is that button's, and it does not show the row as pressed. The focus ring outlines the whole row. On a selected row it is drawn in the ink that reads on the accent, just inside the pill, because a ring in the focus colour would vanish into the accent (and the selected row is a keyboard list's Tab stop).

selected draws the solid accent pill. It is the system's "selected row": it means "this is the current item", such as the channel you are in. Use it on one row of a list. It also tells assistive technology which item is current. On a selected row the text takes the colour that reads on the accent, so unread and muted do not change how it looks.

Kit components in leading and trailing know which layer they sit on. On the accent pill (a selected row) they switch to the colours that read on it: an Icon, Text or ghost or soft IconButton takes the on-accent ink, and an accent Badge or Pill turns round (an on-accent fill with accent text) so it stays visible. A danger Badge and the status Pills keep their own colours. An unselected row does not reset the layer: it keeps what is around it, so a row inside a Card is on the Card (its hover and pressed tint are mixed over the Card's fill, and a soft IconButton in trailing draws on surface). A Menu or Popover opened from a button in the row is its own layer and draws normally, even from a selected row. Content that is not a kit component does not get any of this, so keep it out of the slots of a selected row, or give it colours that read on the accent.

unread makes the main line bolder and brings it to the full text colour. muted dims both lines. Disabled dims the row and a disabled link or button cannot be used.

Prop Values Default Meaning primary text none (required) The main line. It is cut to one line with an ellipsis. secondary text none A second, smaller line. It is cut to one line too. leading an Avatar or an Icon none What sits before the text. See below. trailing a Badge, a Pill or an IconButton none What sits at the end of the row. See below. size md, lg md md is one line high and fully rounded. lg has room for two lines and rounded corners like a card. selected true, false false The current item: the solid accent pill. unread true, false false A bolder main line in the full text colour, and ", unread" in the row's name. trailingLabel text none What the trailing slot means, added to the row's name ("2 mentions", "admin"). See below. muted true, false false Both lines dimmed. disabled true, false false The row is not available. href an address none Makes the row a link. onClick a function none Makes the row a button. strong true, false false The same bold, full-colour primary line as unread, for a title row (the call bar's room), with nothing added to the name. Web kit only so far. label text none The accessible name of the link or button, when its visible lines do not say what it does: the call bar's room row is "Open call view, Squad Up". The naming rule: label replaces the visible lines in the name, then ", unread" and trailingLabel are appended, and the secondary line becomes the description (aria-describedby): a screen reader hears "Open call view, Squad Up, Muted". Without label the name is the visible lines with ", unread" and trailingLabel after the primary. Ignored on a plain row. Web kit only so far. chevron true, false false A chevron (ChevronRight, icon.sm) at the end of the link or button, before trailing: a visible sign, on touch too, that the row goes somewhere. It takes icon.sm + space.sm from the text. Hidden from screen readers. Ignored on a plain row. Web kit only so far. busy true, false false The link or button is working: what it opens is still loading (a tapped channel whose screen is a chunk on its way). It sets aria-busy, shows a small Spinner (icon.sm) at the end of the link or button in place of the chevron, and stays focusable. A busy button ignores presses. Ignored on a plain or disabled row. Stories: kit-list-row--busy, kit-list-row--busy-light, kit-list-row--busy-tinted. Web kit only so far. focus rowFocus(id) from useListFocus none Joins a keyboard list. See below.

leading holds an Avatar (a person or a community) or an Icon (a channel, a setting). The text lines up in the same place whichever you use. trailing holds a Badge for an unread count, a Pill for a short tag, or an IconButton for a row action such as "More". Put one thing there, or a few small ones. The slot takes at most half the row: a long tag (a role written out in full) cuts with an ellipsis instead of squeezing the name (kit-list-row--long-trailing-pill). Web kit only so far; the native kit has not caught up (see Extending the system).

trailing sits outside the row's link or button, so its meaning is not in the row's name. Pass it as words in trailingLabel ("2 mentions", "admin"): the row adds them to its accessible name after the main line, and unread adds ", unread".
